idiom_name: abstract class with a final skeleton over abstract members, or a thin-interface/enrichment trait
implementation_notes: Scala realizes the pattern with an abstract class whose skeleton is a `final def` over abstract and overridable defs, or - more specifically Scala - with a thin interface plus an enrichment trait: the trait declares a small set of abstract members and one concrete method implemented in terms of them, so mixing the trait in supplies the whole algorithm (Odersky's "turning a thin interface into a rich one", the shape used throughout the collections). Stackable traits extend the pattern further: an `abstract override def` step can wrap super and layer behaviour. Keep the final-def skeleton when subclasses must not reorder steps, and remember that trait members can never be final - only a class can close the skeleton.
pitfalls: Trait members cannot be final, so a trait-carried skeleton stays overridable; use an abstract class with a final def when the sequence must hold.
`abstract override` (stackable traits) only works when every layer calls super - a layer that forgets it silently cuts off the layers below, and mixin order decides which layer runs first.
Trait linearisation and early initialisation can run the skeleton before another mixin's state exists, so the skeleton must not depend on fields owned by later mixins.
